newsitem.title: USA: Air cargo industry should stress economic benefits.
newsitem.headline: Air cargo industry should stress economic benefits.

text.p: Airports and cargo executives need to do a better job telling the public about the economic benefits of the industry, speakers at an air cargo conference here urged this week.
"The cargo industry is jobs," Roy Williams, director of Aviation at the Dayton International Airport, told the 150 executives attending the air cargo conference.
"The cargo industry is invisible. One of our important tasks is how do we make cargo visible?" Williams said.
It is not just a U.S. challenge.
"We have to show them (the politicians) the economic argument," Reinger Thomas general manager for freight logistics, Flughafen Frankfurt/Main AG said.
The Frankfurt/Main airport is the biggest employer in the area, even ahead of Volkswagen AG, he said.

"We have to show them again and again," he said, explaining that the community will be more flexible about issues such as night flights and traffic problems if they better undertand the economic benefits cargo provides.
Thomas estimated that for every airport job, 2.1 jobs are generated in the community.

The economic benefits of cargo to local economies must be made clear, Dayton's Williams said, because cargo's older aircraft with their noise and emissions can make them an easy target for regulatory action.

Passengers are not inconvenienced by these actions and nobody understands the negative economic impact, he told the conference sponsored by the Airports Council International-North America, Air Freight Association, and the American Association of Airport Executives.

"If you started opening every passenger's bag for security inspection, a program like that would not last long," Williams said. But if the government requires every box in a cargo shipment to be ripped open, nobody will care, he said.
"If you force a Northwest or Emery to ground a freighter, you are not grounding any Congressmen or Mayors," Williams said.
